title: Memory Utilization & Paging (Windows)
exclusions: Detects sustained, correlated host-level Windows memory pressure from the `Memory` performance object only. It does not equate committed virtual memory with physical RAM, treat `Available MBytes` as a percentage, or treat `Pages/sec` as page-file traffic alone. It does not identify the consuming process, distinguish file-backed hard faults from page-file I/O, measure private bytes, working sets, pools, NUMA locality, guest ballooning, Hyper-V dynamic-memory demand, container limits, application allocation failures, or page-file disk latency. The primary alert requires three complete five-minute buckets in which average `% Committed Bytes In Use` is at least 80 percentage points, average `Available MBytes` is below 500 MB, and average `Pages/sec` is greater than 1,000 pages/second. It intentionally does not alert on any one counter alone. Missing, stale, localized, malformed, duplicate, unit-inconsistent, or incomplete counter collection is telemetry failure, not healthy memory. No exception lookup is applied by the base SPL, and this operational use case provides no security, adversary-attribution, remediation, or regulatory-attestation claim.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `windows_sustained_memory_pressure` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, fixed time bounds, dispatch history, and alert-action configuration; effective `Splunk_TA_windows/local/inputs.conf` and `btool` output; add-on, forwarder, Windows, and Splunk platform versions; expected-host inventory; source-health results for all five required counters; and exported alert rows containing host, pressure interval, qualifying bucket count, committed percentage, committed and limit GiB, available MB, pages/second, and percentage-reconciliation delta. Preserve the corresponding raw `Perfmon:Memory` events, contemporaneous Windows Performance Monitor or `Get-Counter` output, incident/change record, bounded exception record if notification was suppressed, and dated positive/negative control results. These artifacts demonstrate that indexed samples met the documented correlation rule; they do not prove root cause, page-file-only I/O, process ownership, remediation, or uninterrupted fleet coverage. This documentation-only review created no runtime evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated event index with fixed absolute times spanning exactly three completed five-minute buckets, ingest one `Perfmon:Memory` event per minute for each of the five required counters on `host=win-memory-positive`. For every sample set `% Committed Bytes In Use=87.5`, `Committed Bytes=15032385536`, `Commit Limit=17179869184`, `Available MBytes=400`, and `Pages/sec=1200`; set `object=Memory`, numeric `Value`, and the production field names. Point a copy of the SPL at the fixture index and equivalent fixed bounds. Expect exactly one row: `qualifying_buckets=3`, `peak_committed_pct=87.5`, committed 14 GiB, commit limit 16 GiB, `lowest_available_mb=400`, `peak_pages_per_sec=1200`, and percentage delta 0.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated fixed-time variants and expect zero alert rows for each: high `Pages/sec=1500` with 8,192 available MB and 50% committed; 90% committed with 400 available MB but `Pages/sec=100`; all three thresholds in only two buckets; fewer than four samples for any required counter in one bucket; `Commit Limit=0`; a negative value; native committed percentage of 90 while `Committed Bytes/Commit Limit` derives 50% (delta over two points); a localized or misspelled counter name; and events outside the delayed search window. Verify a separate source-health search identifies incomplete, invalid, missing, localized, duplicate-stanza, and stale inputs rather than interpreting their zero alert output as healthy.

dataSources: Primary source: local Windows Performance Data Helper counters collected by the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) through a `[perfmon://Memory]` input in `mode=single`, routed by local convention to `index=perfmon sourcetype=Perfmon:Memory` every 60 seconds. Required `Memory` counters are `% Committed Bytes In Use` (percentage points of system commit limit), `Committed Bytes` and `Commit Limit` (bytes), `Available MBytes` (megabytes of immediately available physical memory), and `Pages/sec` (pages read from or written to disk to resolve hard faults, including file-backed activity). Splunk metadata supplies `_time` and `host`; event fields are `object`, `counter`, and numeric `Value`. `useEnglishOnly=true` stabilizes the exact English object and counter names across Windows locales. The index name is configurable but must match the SPL.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for supported local Windows `perfmon://` collection and search-time knowledge. Deploy collection configuration to Windows Universal Forwarders or full Splunk Enterprise instances, and deploy the add-on's parsing/search knowledge to the tiers required by the topology. The Universal Forwarder is the execution tier, not the add-on and not Splunkbase app 617.
spl:
index=perfmon sourcetype="Perfmon:Memory" object="Memory" counter IN ("% Committed Bytes In Use","Committed Bytes","Commit Limit","Available MBytes","Pages/sec") earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval committed_pct_sample=if(counter=="% Committed Bytes In Use",tonumber(Value),null()), committed_bytes_sample=if(counter=="Committed Bytes",tonumber(Value),null()), commit_limit_bytes_sample=if(counter=="Commit Limit",tonumber(Value),null()), available_mb_sample=if(counter=="Available MBytes",tonumber(Value),null()), pages_per_sec_sample=if(counter=="Pages/sec",tonumber(Value),null())
| bin _time span=5m
| stats avg(committed_pct_sample) as committed_pct avg(committed_bytes_sample) as committed_bytes avg(commit_limit_bytes_sample) as commit_limit_bytes avg(available_mb_sample) as available_mb avg(pages_per_sec_sample) as pages_per_sec count(committed_pct_sample) as committed_pct_samples count(committed_bytes_sample) as committed_bytes_samples count(commit_limit_bytes_sample) as commit_limit_samples count(available_mb_sample) as available_mb_samples count(pages_per_sec_sample) as pages_per_sec_samples by _time host
| where committed_pct_samples>=4 AND committed_bytes_samples>=4 AND commit_limit_samples>=4 AND available_mb_samples>=4 AND pages_per_sec_samples>=4 AND committed_pct>=0 AND committed_pct<=100 AND committed_bytes>=0 AND commit_limit_bytes>0 AND available_mb>=0 AND pages_per_sec>=0
| eval derived_committed_pct=100*committed_bytes/commit_limit_bytes, committed_pct_delta=abs(committed_pct-derived_committed_pct)
| where committed_pct_delta<=2
| eval committed_pct=round(committed_pct,2), committed_gib=round(committed_bytes/pow(1024,3),2), commit_limit_gib=round(commit_limit_bytes/pow(1024,3),2), available_mb=round(available_mb,2), pages_per_sec=round(pages_per_sec,2), committed_pct_delta=round(committed_pct_delta,2)
| where committed_pct>=80 AND available_mb<500 AND pages_per_sec>1000
| stats count as qualifying_buckets min(_time) as pressure_start max(_time) as last_qualifying_bucket max(committed_pct) as peak_committed_pct max(committed_gib) as peak_committed_gib max(commit_limit_gib) as peak_commit_limit_gib min(available_mb) as lowest_available_mb max(pages_per_sec) as peak_pages_per_sec max(committed_pct_delta) as max_committed_pct_delta by host
| where qualifying_buckets=3
| eval pressure_end=last_qualifying_bucket+300, severity="critical", use_case="UC-1.2.2"
| table pressure_start pressure_end host severity qualifying_buckets peak_committed_pct peak_committed_gib peak_commit_limit_gib lowest_available_mb peak_pages_per_sec max_committed_pct_delta use_case
| sort 0 -peak_committed_pct lowest_available_mb host
description: Identifies sustained, severe Windows memory pressure by correlating three different resource signals across three complete five-minute buckets. It measures system commit consumption against the commit limit, physical memory immediately available in MB, and hard-page disk transfers in pages/second, while cross-checking the native committed percentage against `Committed Bytes / Commit Limit` and failing closed on incomplete counter sets.
value: Correlated warning reduces two costly errors: missing a host approaching commit exhaustion and paging-driven latency, and paging responders for a single misleading counter. Requiring high commit use, very low available physical memory, and elevated hard faults gives Windows and application teams a defensible incident signal while retaining the absolute values needed to size capacity, inspect consumers, and challenge the diagnosis.
implementation: Install `Splunk_TA_windows` on qualified Windows collection tiers and enable one local `[perfmon://Memory]` stanza with the five explicit English counters, `mode=single`, `interval=60`, and `index=perfmon`. Validate counter names, units, event shape, cadence, host identity, and completeness before saving the SPL as `windows_sustained_memory_pressure`. Schedule it every five minutes; it evaluates three completed buckets after a five-minute ingestion delay and alerts only when all three documented thresholds persist.
visualization: Lead with source health: expected hosts missing any required counter, per-counter sample counts, newest event age, and duplicate-stanza indicators. For qualified hosts, show separate unit-labelled panels for `% Committed Bytes In Use` (percentage points), `Committed Bytes` and `Commit Limit` (GiB), `Available MBytes` (MB), and `Pages/sec` (pages/s); never place these raw values on one unlabeled axis. Use a three-panel synchronized 24-hour timechart with horizontal policy lines at 80%, 500 MB, and 1,000 pages/s, plus a table matching the alert output and drilldowns to all five raw counters, process `Private Bytes`/`Working Set` context, paging-file disk latency, and Windows native counter output. Display gaps as unknown, not zero.
schema: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows Perfmon event fields plus Windows Memory performance-counter semantics; partial CIM Performance.Memory context
dataModelAcceleration: CIM Performance.Memory can represent `mem_committed` and memory-capacity fields in megabytes, but it does not preserve the Windows commit limit, `% Committed Bytes In Use`, `Pages/sec`, the raw counter identity, five-counter bucket completeness, or native-versus-derived percentage reconciliation required by this alert. `mem_free` is also not automatically equivalent to Windows `Available MBytes` unless the installed add-on mapping is verified. No semantically equivalent `cimSpl` or accelerated `tstats` alert is claimed. A summary index may be used at fleet scale only if it retains all five measurements, their units, bucket/sample completeness, host/time identity, and reconciliation gates.

knownFalsePositives:
The correlation rule is deliberately stricter than a one-counter alert, but it can still identify a real measurement condition whose cause is expected or whose impact is acceptable.

1. **Approved load or capacity test** — A soak test, failover exercise, cache warm-up, or deliberate overcommit test can drive all three counters through the rule. Confirm the exact host set, test owner, approved UTC interval, expected allocation profile, and recovery criteria. Preserve the alert as control evidence; suppress only notification for the bounded test.

2. **Backup, antivirus, search indexing, or memory-mapped file scan** — `Pages/sec` includes hard faults for file-backed mappings and filesystem cache, not only page-file reads/writes. A backup or scanner can therefore raise it while other memory signals are also stressed. Correlate `Pages Input/sec`, `Pages Output/sec`, paging-file disk I/O, Process Monitor or Windows Performance Recorder evidence, process working sets/private bytes, and the job schedule before asserting page-file thrashing.

3. **Planned service startup, failover, or node rejoin** — Database buffer pools, Java or .NET heaps, analytics engines, and clustered services can commit memory rapidly and fault working sets during initialization. Check service lifecycle, expected steady-state commit, recovery duration, and peer capacity. Repeated or prolonged pressure after warm-up remains actionable.

4. **Host role and memory-size diversity** — The absolute 500 MB boundary is the explicit absolute branch of current Microsoft critical guidance; it is not 10% and can be too late as a local operating threshold on large servers. Conversely, a small lab host may cross it during supported work. If policy needs a relative available-memory rule, join a validated physical-RAM inventory and create a separately named/tested percentage field; never divide `Available MBytes` by `Commit Limit`.

5. **System-managed page-file expansion or change** — Windows can expand a system-managed page file, changing `Commit Limit` during the observation. This can lower `% Committed Bytes In Use` even while `Committed Bytes` grows, or create transient reconciliation differences between asynchronously sampled counters. Inspect the five raw series, page-file configuration/change history, and bucket-level delta. Do not disable the reconciliation gate to make the alert fire.

6. **Virtual-machine memory operations** — Hyper-V dynamic memory, hypervisor ballooning, host reclamation, snapshot restore, live migration, or guest restart can produce genuine guest pressure without an in-guest process leak. Correlate hypervisor-assigned/demand memory and migration events. This use case observes the guest or host Windows counter context where the collector runs; it does not infer physical-host capacity.

7. **Counter reset, boot, or partial startup bucket** — Service restart, host boot, add-on deployment, or forwarding recovery can produce sparse buckets or discontinuities. The SPL requires four samples of every counter and three qualified buckets, but duplicated stanzas can satisfy counts artificially. Check boot time, effective input, raw event multiplicity, and event age before escalation.

8. **Collection replay or duplicate input stanza** — Duplicate app assignments, local plus deployment-server stanzas, or replayed queues can alter averages and sample counts. Compare expected 60-second cadence, `_indextime`, raw event identity, forwarder GUID, and `btool` precedence. Repair collection instead of deduplicating unknown measurements in the alert.

9. **Localized or locally renamed counter configuration** — Without `useEnglishOnly=true`, non-English object/counter names do not match the SPL. A local alias or custom sourcetype can produce apparently missing data. Treat that as source failure; validate with `typeperf -qx` or `Get-Counter -ListSet Memory` on the host and restore a version-controlled English input contract.

10. **Short incident already recovering** — The search intentionally requires 15 sustained minutes and can miss a shorter but severe allocation failure. Fast application out-of-memory detection, Windows event logs, service health, and process-specific controls are complementary. Do not weaken persistence globally to cover a different failure mode.

**Safe suppression:** keep the base search and source-health controls unchanged. If notification suppression is required, apply a separate `windows_memory_pressure_exceptions.csv` lookup after the final result, keyed by exact `host` and `policy_id`, with numeric `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject wildcards, open-ended entries, and exceptions for missing or invalid telemetry. Retain suppressed results and review expired entries.

cost.search_load_notes: At a 60-second interval in single-event mode, five counters produce approximately 7,200 small events per host per day. The five-minute scheduled alert scans a delayed 15-minute measurement window, aggregates at most three buckets per host, and performs no join, subsearch, transaction, or high-cardinality instance split.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement contract

Assign a Windows platform owner, Splunk collection owner, search-content owner, application escalation path, and page-file/storage escalation path. Install a currently supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) on the Windows collection tier and make its parsing and search-time knowledge available wherever the topology requires it. Use a Universal Forwarder or full Splunk Enterprise instance that can read local Windows performance counters and forward to the approved index. The search role needs read access to that event index and permission to save and schedule a search; alert-action credentials should be separately constrained. No domain administrator, remote WMI, registry-write, process-termination, page-file-change, or debugging privilege is required for this read-only control.

The five counters answer different questions and their units must never be merged. `Committed Bytes` is system committed virtual memory in **bytes**: allocations for which Windows must be able to provide backing in RAM or paging files. `Commit Limit` is the current maximum system commit capacity, broadly tied to RAM plus paging-file backing and capable of changing when a system-managed page file changes. `% Committed Bytes In Use` is a **percentage**, approximately `100 * Committed Bytes / Commit Limit`; it is not physical-RAM utilization. The SPL retains both source values and rejects a bucket when the native and derived percentages differ by more than two percentage points.

`Available MBytes` is immediately available **physical** memory in megabytes, including reclaimable standby, free, and zero-page lists. It is neither committed memory nor a percent. The alert uses less than 500 MB because current Microsoft Windows Server guidance explicitly identifies less than 1% **or** less than 500 MB as critical; without a trustworthy total-physical-memory field this use case can implement only the absolute branch. It does not pretend that 500 MB equals 10% on every host. A deployment that needs a relative rule must join a versioned physical-memory inventory and calculate `100 * Available MBytes / physical_ram_mb` in separately named content.

`Pages/sec` is a rate in **pages per second** for pages read from or written to disk to resolve hard faults. It includes file-backed and memory-mapped activity and is not equivalent to paging-file I/O, page-file percentage used, megabytes per second, or soft page faults. Microsoft PAL guidance uses greater than 1,000 pages/second as a high threshold and explicitly says to correlate it with available-memory and leak evidence. This use case therefore requires high commit consumption and very low physical availability at the same time. The 80% commit boundary and 500 MB available boundary come from current Microsoft threshold guidance; the 1,000 pages/second boundary is a starting triage policy, not a hardware-independent law.

The temporal contract is also explicit. A 60-second input should provide about five samples of each counter per five-minute bucket. Each bucket needs at least four valid samples of every counter. The search inspects three completed buckets from 20 minutes ago through five minutes ago, tolerating one missed sample per counter per bucket and a five-minute indexing delay. All three buckets must satisfy all three thresholds. Missing counters fail closed and must be reported by a separate health search. `index=perfmon`, 60 seconds, two-percentage-point reconciliation tolerance, four samples, five-minute buckets, 15-minute persistence, and five-minute delay are deployment policy values; change them only with versioned tests and evidence.

## Step 1 — Configure the supported Windows counter input

Do not edit `Splunk_TA_windows/default`. Create or update `%SPLUNK_HOME%\etc\apps\Splunk_TA_windows\local\inputs.conf` through the deployment server or the approved local app. Use one authoritative stanza:

```ini
[perfmon://Memory]
disabled = 0
object = Memory
counters = % Committed Bytes In Use; Committed Bytes; Commit Limit; Available MBytes; Pages/sec
interval = 60
mode = single
useEnglishOnly = true
index = perfmon
sourcetype = Perfmon:Memory
```

`mode=single` gives the alert one event with `object`, `counter`, and `Value` for each sampled counter. Keep this event-index contract separate from an ITSI metric-index configuration such as `PerfmonMetrics:Memory`; an `mstats` implementation would be different content. `useEnglishOnly=true` invokes the English Windows counter API and requires explicit English object/counter names; do not replace them with wildcards or regular expressions. The `Memory` object has no per-process or disk instance, so no `instances=*` setting is needed. Collect process and paging-file diagnostics in separately governed inputs because wildcard process counters can create substantial volume.

Deploy collection to representative Windows hosts first. Restart the forwarder when required by the platform procedure. On each canary inspect the effective stanza with:

```powershell
& "$env:SPLUNK_HOME\bin\splunk.exe" btool inputs list perfmon://Memory --debug
```

Confirm one winning stanza, the intended app path, one index, 60-second interval, single mode, and no local/deployment duplicate. Verify the Windows service identity can enumerate the counters with `Get-Counter -ListSet Memory` and can sample them:

```powershell
Get-Counter '\Memory\% Committed Bytes In Use','\Memory\Committed Bytes','\Memory\Commit Limit','\Memory\Available MBytes','\Memory\Pages/sec' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 3
```

Use the native command only for qualification and incident comparison; do not add a second scripted input for the same measurements. Confirm host metadata is stable and unique, system time is synchronized, output queues are healthy, and the target index exists and is searchable. At one event per counter per minute, expect about 7,200 events per host per day. Measure actual bytes and forwarder CPU on canaries before broad rollout.

## Step 2 — Validate ingestion, field shape, units, and source health

Run this qualification search over at least 30 minutes:

```spl
index=perfmon sourcetype="Perfmon:Memory" object="Memory" counter IN ("% Committed Bytes In Use","Committed Bytes","Commit Limit","Available MBytes","Pages/sec") earliest=-30m
| eval numeric_value=tonumber(Value)
| stats count min(numeric_value) as minimum max(numeric_value) as maximum latest(_time) as newest dc(counter) as distinct_counters by host counter
| eval age_seconds=now()-newest
| sort 0 host counter
```

For every expected host require five counter rows, numeric values, roughly 30 observations per counter, and a newest event within two intervals plus measured indexing delay. `% Committed Bytes In Use` should remain between zero and 100; byte, MB, and rate values must be nonnegative; `Commit Limit` must be positive. Check raw events to confirm `Value` has not been converted to a unit-bearing string and that `_time` follows collection time. Compare with the Windows Performance Monitor interface on the same host: use **Performance Monitor > Monitoring Tools > Performance Monitor** beside the indexed sample set and the five-counter `Get-Counter` output. Small differences are expected when the samples are not simultaneous; units and order of magnitude must agree.

Task Manager **Performance > Memory > Committed** is useful corroboration for current committed/limit values but is not the authoritative source for exact sampled timestamps or every counter. Never compare `Available MBytes` directly to Task Manager's used-memory percentage, and never interpret a large `Committed Bytes` value as bytes resident in RAM. Divide bytes by `1024^3` only for a GiB display. Leave threshold arithmetic in native percentage points, MB, and pages/second.

Create a source-health report independent of the alert. Maintain an expected-host inventory and report: no `Perfmon:Memory` event; fewer than five exact counter names; stale newest sample; fewer or many more than expected samples; nonnumeric, negative, or impossible values; zero commit limit; native/derived commit discrepancy; localized names; wrong object/source type/index; duplicate effective stanza; forwarder queue delay; host-identity collision; and a host newly absent after decommission without inventory approval. A silent primary search is not source-health evidence. Do not use `fillnull value=0` for a missing counter because zero available memory or commit limit has operational meaning and a fabricated zero can create or hide an alert.

## Step 3 — Create and understand the sustained correlation alert

Save the catalogue SPL as `windows_sustained_memory_pressure`. Schedule it every five minutes on a five-minute boundary and trigger when result count is greater than zero. Keep `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m` in the SPL or move equivalent fixed bounds to the saved-search configuration, but do not apply both conflicting windows. The latest five minutes are intentionally excluded to allow indexing to finish; measure fleet p95 delay and change the delay only with source-health and fixture tests.

The base search selects only the exact event-index, source-type, object, and five-counter contract. The first `eval` creates one unit-specific field per counter and converts `Value` to a number. Nulls remain null. `bin` assigns events to five-minute boundaries. `stats` averages each metric and counts its nonnull samples by host and bucket. The validity gate requires four samples of every counter, a percentage from zero through 100, nonnegative measurements, and a positive commit limit.

The search derives committed percentage from the averaged byte counters and compares it with the averaged native percentage. A difference over two percentage points rejects the bucket. This tolerance accommodates slightly asynchronous counter events and rounding but still catches extraction/unit drift or a rapidly changing commit limit that makes the aggregate unsafe. Inspect rejected buckets in source health rather than widening the tolerance automatically.

Only complete, reconciled buckets are tested against policy: committed percentage at least 80, available physical memory below 500 MB, and Pages/sec greater than 1,000. All three conditions are joined with `AND`; high paging alone is not enough. The final `stats` counts qualifying buckets. Exactly three exist in the fixed 15-minute measurement window, and all three must qualify. `pressure_start` is the first bucket start and `pressure_end` is five minutes after the last bucket start. Output GiB values are display conversions from bytes; they are not fed back into threshold logic.

Start with one alert result per host and route it to Windows/platform operations. Do not call the rule “memory utilization above 90%”: it is a correlated commit, physical-availability, and hard-fault rule. If the organization needs an earlier warning, create a separate report or tested policy, for example relative available-memory percentage derived from physical-RAM inventory or a rising commit trend. Do not turn this critical rule into `OR` logic or page on `Pages/sec` alone. Keep process-level attribution and page-file disk diagnostics as drilldowns, not assumptions in the alert title.

## Step 4 — Test logic, native truth, and failure behavior

Use absolute fixture times and an isolated event index. Load the positive scenario's 75 events: five counters, five one-minute samples, three buckets. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds replacing the relative bounds. Assert one row and every exact expected result. Inspect the bucket table before the final aggregation and prove each counter count is five, the derived percentage is 87.5, the delta is zero, and every threshold is satisfied.

Run every negative variant independently. High paging with ample available memory must not alert because hard faults can be file-backed. High commit and low availability with low paging must not alert under this specific severe-correlation contract; it should remain visible on dashboards and may be handled by a separate commit-exhaustion policy. Two qualifying buckets must not satisfy 15-minute persistence. Three samples for one counter, zero commit limit, negative values, native/derived disagreement, localized names, and out-of-window events must all produce zero primary rows and positive source-health findings where applicable.

Test exact boundaries: 80 committed qualifies, 79.99 does not; 499.99 available qualifies, 500 does not; 1,000 Pages/sec does not, 1,000.01 does. A two-point percentage delta qualifies and a value above two does not. Test four versus three samples. Confirm the fixed window creates exactly three buckets on the actual scheduler. Test delayed indexing by adding events after the five-minute close delay and ensure source health reports lag rather than silently extending the window.

On a Windows canary, compare indexed samples with `Get-Counter` and Performance Monitor during normal operation and a safe, approved lab pressure test. Do not exhaust memory or disable the page file on a shared or production host merely to fire the alert. A synthetic event fixture proves SPL arithmetic and gates; a safe canary comparison proves collection and units; neither proves that the starting thresholds fit every workload. Record tester, dates, Windows/add-on/forwarder/search-platform versions, fixture checksum, exact time bounds, expected and actual rows, alert delivery, and exceptions. Keep `status=draft` until runtime, workload-owner, and operations acceptance is complete.

## Step 5 — Operationalize response, dashboards, and evidence

Build the unit-separated dashboard described in `visualization`. Put source health and missing-host inventory first. Show commit percentage beside absolute committed/limit GiB so a responder can see both ratio and scale. Show available MB independently. Show Pages/sec with clear help text that it includes file-backed hard faults. Plot gaps as null and overlay deployment, reboot, failover, backup, antivirus, and capacity-test annotations where available. Restrict raw host telemetry and process drilldowns according to infrastructure-data policy; result-only access may be broader.

When the alert fires, first confirm three complete buckets, five counters, current source health, host identity, boot/change context, and the native/derived percentage delta. Then compare current `Get-Counter` or Performance Monitor values. In Task Manager or approved process telemetry, inspect process **Commit size/Private Bytes** and **Working Set** as different quantities. Correlate `Pages Input/sec`, `Pages Output/sec`, paging-file disk operations/latency, application allocation or out-of-memory events, service restarts, pool usage, hypervisor dynamic-memory/ballooning data, and scheduled backup or scanning activity. `Pages/sec` alone cannot identify `pagefile.sys`; use approved Windows Performance Recorder/Analyzer, Process Monitor, or storage telemetry when root-cause detail is required.

Do not automatically kill a process, restart a service, clear a cache, resize or disable a page file, add RAM, change application heap limits, or migrate a virtual machine from this alert. Those actions can cause outages, alter the commit limit during evidence collection, or hide a leak. Follow the application/Windows runbook, preserve before-state evidence, obtain change approval, and verify recovery in all five counters plus service-level latency/error indicators. If committed bytes continue rising, investigate process private bytes and kernel pools; if paging is high but memory recovers, investigate file-backed activity and disk impact; if available memory stays low without paging, review workload design and a separate capacity policy.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` under the local operations policy. The 30-day warm-retention value in `cost` is an estimate, not a mandate. Review thresholds, delay, sample minimum, host inventory, input ownership, dashboard labels, exceptions, and runbooks after Windows, add-on, forwarder, page-file policy, hypervisor, host-size, or major workload changes. Re-run positive/negative controls after any SPL, field extraction, mode, source type, interval, index, or counter-list change.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot without fabricating health

- **No `Perfmon:Memory` events:** verify add-on assignment, `disabled=0`, Windows service status, effective `btool` stanza, index existence/routing, output queues, and search-role access. Inspect `splunkd.log` for the exact `perfmon://Memory` input. Do not point the search at WMI memory events and claim equivalence.
- **Counter names are localized or missing:** confirm `useEnglishOnly=true`, explicit English names, and that Windows exposes them through `Get-Counter -ListSet Memory` or `typeperf -qx`. English-only mode does not permit object/counter wildcards. Repair the input contract rather than broadening SPL to arbitrary translated strings.
- **Events use `PerfmonMk:Memory` or contain multiple rows:** collection is in multikv mode or follows a different add-on contract. Either restore the documented `mode=single` event feed or author and test a separate normalization. Do not assume `counter` and `Value` have the same cardinality.
- **Events use `PerfmonMetrics:Memory`:** that is a metric-index/ITSI pattern. Use `mstats` and a separately validated metric-name/unit contract; the raw-event SPL is not interchangeable.
- **One counter has fewer samples:** inspect collection duration, queue delay, counter availability, input errors, and `_time` versus `_indextime`. Keep the four-sample gate. Missing commit limit or available memory cannot be inferred from another counter.
- **Native and derived committed percentages disagree:** inspect exact timestamps, counter duplication, byte units, a changing system-managed page file, extraction cardinality, and raw values. Do not compare `Committed Bytes` with physical RAM or convert bytes as decimal GB before deriving the ratio.
- **`Available MBytes` looks too low or high:** compare the same-time native counter, not free-memory or used-percent UI values. Confirm MB units and host identity. Available memory includes reclaimable standby pages; it is not only the free list.
- **`Pages/sec` is high but no alert appears:** expected when commit or available-memory conditions do not also qualify. Investigate mapped-file, backup, antivirus, and cache activity plus disk latency; do not weaken the base rule solely to reproduce a one-counter alarm.
- **An obvious memory incident does not alert:** check whether it lasted less than 15 minutes, involved only commit exhaustion or only low physical memory, occurred in the excluded newest five minutes, lacked complete telemetry, or produced application out-of-memory before paging rose. Deploy complementary fast-failure and source-health controls instead of relabeling this contract.
- **Too many alerts after deployment:** check duplicate stanzas, tests/backups, host-size policy, system-managed page-file changes, virtualization operations, and scheduler/window alignment before changing thresholds. Compare all five bucket series and KFP cases.
- **CIM/tstats does not reproduce the rule:** expected. CIM Performance lacks the complete Windows counter and reconciliation contract. Preserve the raw-event search or build a purpose-specific summary that retains every required invariant.
grandmaExplanation: We watch three different warning signs that a Windows computer is running dangerously short of usable memory, and we wait until they stay bad together before sounding the alarm. This helps the team act on a real sustained problem instead of one misleading number.
